evidence_quotes.quote: As reflected in the two tables, most of the initiatives found take place outside the health system and are focused on social determinants of health affecting low income communities, particularly water, sanitation, waste management, energy, land, biodiversity, UA and food safety and security.

They included investments in leadership and collective organisation; bringing multiple forms of evidence to planning, including from participatory assessment; building co-design and collaboration across multiple sectors, actors and disciplines; and having credible brokers and processes to catalyse and sustain change.

In Epworth, a peri-urban, high density low income settlement in Harare metropolitan area, efforts to address deficits in clean water and sanitation in this water-scarce area called for new, water-conserving sanitation technology.

Rather than a systematic review, we used a focused narrative review, followed by structured case studies and content analysis as described below, given the largely qualitative, diverse, and non-biomedical nature of the evidence (24–26).

The full versions of the 10 case studies are separately provided (28–31), and a comprehensive report provides detailed information on the methods and empirical findings on the initiatives from both the document review and the case studies (27).

criterion_notes.c1: Partially satisfied within a broad multi-sector urban health review: two of the ten summarized case studies (Epworth in Harare, Zimbabwe and informal settlements in Kampala, Uganda) and a subset of desk-reviewed papers concern community water and sanitation initiatives alongside urban agriculture, primary health care, waste management, food vendors, and public spaces.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: This paper PASSES the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 because it discusses participatory governance, community-local authority engagement, multi-stakeholder platforms, and community contracting across urban health initiatives, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because its water and sanitation content examines generic NGO/community project delivery, social mobilization, and technology demonstration (piloting water-conserving toilets with a lending group and youth pump minders in Epworth; community contracting of local builders in Kampala) with only unanalysed one-line tabular mentions of project authorization delays and participatory NGO beneficiary targeting, rather than analyzing a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. Note that plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because the paper independently fails Criteria 4 and 5 (no disaggregated empirical WASH access outcomes or identifiable WASH sample-exposure-outcome data in this overview article).
criterion_notes.c3: Uses a multi-method qualitative approach combining a non-systematic focused narrative review of 52 documents with a manual thematic content analysis of 10 structured case studies informed by 122 documents and 34 key informant interviews across four cities (though detailed empirical findings of the individual case studies are published separately in cited grey-literature reports).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports cross-cutting qualitative themes on participatory, recognitional, distributional, structural, and intergenerational equity and general social/material changes pooled across all 52 documents and 10 multi-sector urban health initiatives, without reporting specific empirical household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (mentioning only that a water-conserving toilet innovation was piloted in 30 Epworth households and that relative distributional outcomes were poorly captured).
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis in this overview article is the urban health/wellbeing initiative pooled across diverse sectors (predominantly urban agriculture, primary health care, food systems, and solid waste); the article does not provide sufficient disaggregated information to identify a specific water/sanitation study population/sample, governance exposure, and WASH service access outcome, explicitly referring readers to separate reports (refs 27-31) for detailed case-study methods and empirical findings.

study_design: Multi-method qualitative thematic review (focused narrative desk review of 52 documents and cross-case content analysis of 10 case studies drawing on 122 documents and 34 key informant interviews)
country: East and Southern Africa (desk review across 12 countries: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe; 10 case studies in Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe)
population_and_sample: 52 documents from online searches (64 urban health/wellbeing examples across 12 ESA countries) and 10 purposively selected urban initiatives in 4 cities (Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, Nairobi) informed by 122 documents and 34 key informant interviews; unit of analysis is the urban initiative
exposure: Features and enablers of community-engaged urban health and wellbeing initiatives (collective organization, participatory mapping/assessment, multi-sector co-design, technology demonstration, and catalytic brokers)
outcome: Qualitative themes across five dimensions of equity (participatory, recognitional, distributional, structural, and intergenerational equity) and broad social, material, and system changes across multi-sector urban health initiatives (no disaggregated empirical WASH access outcomes reported)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure), with secondary failures on Criteria 4 and 5. This Frontiers in Public Health 'Policy and Practice Review' conducts a non-systematic focused narrative review of 52 documents and a cross-case thematic content analysis of 10 urban health and wellbeing initiatives in East and Southern Africa (predominantly covering urban agriculture, primary health care committees, solid waste/briquettes, food vendor mapping, and public spaces, alongside 2 community WASH initiatives in Epworth, Harare and informal settlements in Kampala). Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, the paper examines generic community-engaged project delivery, social mobilization, multi-stakeholder collaboration, and pilot technology demonstration (e.g., demonstrating water-conserving toilets in 30 pilot households with a lending group and youth pump minders in Epworth; community contracting of local builders in Kampala) rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access. Furthermore, even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded because it synthesizes broad equity themes across multi-sector initiatives without reporting disaggregated empirical water or sanitation access outcomes (c4) or sufficient case-level population, exposure, and WASH outcome detail (c5), referring readers to separate grey-literature reports (refs 27-31) for empirical case-study findings.
